candidates.title: HGRL-ATN: a hierarchical graph reinforcement learning framework for trustworthy UAV navigation under GPS spoofing attacks
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) that rely on the Global Positioning System (GPS) for localization are increasingly exposed to spoofing attacks that induce large positional deviations and mission failure. Established defense model-based estimators, Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) sensor fusion, and standard deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-are largely reactive, generalize poorly to unseen attack patterns, and do not model the relational structure that links heterogeneous sensor modalities. This paper presents HGRL-ATN, a framework that couples graph-neural-network (GNN) sensor fusion, variational trust estimation, and hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) into a single end-to-end pipeline for secure UAV navigation. Sensors are represented as nodes of a graph and fused by a graph attention network, allowing cross-modal inconsistencies induced by spoofing to be detected relationally. A variational module assigns per-sensor trust and uncertainty scores that down-weight compromised inputs, while a two-level policy separates navigation strategy selection from continuous control. A digital-twin module predicts next-state dynamics to support anticipatory decision making. Evaluated on a synthetic UAV dataset, the VeReMi benchmark, and CARLA-generated scenarios, HGRL-ATN attains a detection accuracy of 97.0\%, an F1-score of 0.965, and a navigation success rate of 94.8\%, against 82.3\%--90.4\% for representative baselines. Ablation confirms that graph fusion and trust estimation are the dominant contributors, and trajectory analysis shows substantially reduced path deviation under active spoofing.

candidates.title: A systematic investigation of age-gender intersectional stereotypes and their consequences
candidates.abstract: Research on age and gender stereotypes has largely examined these dimensions in isolation or reduced their intersection to broad perceptions of warmth and competence. To foster a more nuanced understanding of age-gender intersecting stereotypes, the present research offers a systematic, inductive-deductive investigation of stereotype content toward individuals with intersecting age and gender identities. Using exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, Study 1 inductively develops and validates six target-specific stereotype measurement models comprising 22 stereotype dimensions capturing mixed-valence content of younger, middle-aged, and older women and men. Study 2 uses a deductive approach to categorize these dimensions into a framework distinguishing interactive, additive, age-based, and gender-based stereotypes, with multiple interactive or additive stereotypes emerging for each age-gender target. Study 3 establishes the convergent and discriminant validity of these dimensions and finds evidence that some dimensions predict attitudes beyond established models of person perception. Finally, Study 4 demonstrates that age-gender targets are differentially assigned to organizational roles that align with stereotype content associated with their groups and that role-relevant stereotype dimensions predict hiring decisions beyond broader perceptions of warmth and competence. Overall, the present studies highlight the complex interplay between age and gender in shaping stereotype content, show the consequences of these stereotypes in real-world contexts, contribute to ongoing social-psychological arguments for going beyond warmth and competence in stereotype models, and ultimately, lay essential groundwork for further empirical investigations on an increasingly timely topic. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

candidates.title: THE KHÁNH INTELLIGENCE MATRIX (TKI MATRIX) A Bottom-Up Interdisciplinary Research Framework for Intelligence Recognition in Biological and Social Systems
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: Intelligence is commonly investigated through cognitive abilities, learning performance, adaptation, problem-solving and measurable behavioural outcomes. However, an additional question deserves systematic investigation: how do biological and social systems recognize, evaluate and respond to intelligence? The recognition of intelligence may influence whom individuals learn from, whose knowledge they trust, how knowledge is distributed and whether a system rewards genuine competence or merely the appearance of competence. This paper introduces the Khánh Intelligence Matrix (TKI Matrix), an interdisciplinary research framework designed to investigate intelligence recognition through a bottom-up approach. Rather than beginning with a universal definition or a predetermined classification of intelligence, the framework begins with observable mechanisms and measurable interactions at biological, individual, interpersonal and collective levels. The framework distinguishes actual competence, self-assessed competence, recognition received from others, reputation, recognition motivation and subsequent learning behaviour. It proposes twelve initial research variables, ten research questions and six falsifiable hypotheses. Three complementary research programmes are outlined: controlled human experiments, comparative animal social-learning studies and agent-based computational simulations. The central proposition is that recognition and competence are related but not necessarily identical. When recognition becomes detached from demonstrated competence, systems may develop feedback loops that favour reputation, status or performance displays over learning and error correction. This proposition remains an empirical research question rather than an established universal law. The TKI Matrix aims to provide a revisable research architecture for understanding how intelligence is recognized and how recognition mechanisms influence the development of knowledge across biological and social systems.

candidates.title: Auditing the Auditor: Extraction Accuracy, Hallucination, and Abstention in Open-Weight LLMs for ESG Reporting A Longitudinal Empirical Benchmark Across 518 Corporate Disclosures (2010–2026)
candidates.abstract: Abstract  Corporate sustainability auditing increasingly relies on Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract verified quantitative metrics from lengthy Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) reports. For an LLM to serve as a trustworthy compliance tool, it must pull exact numbers from dense ta- bles while refusing to guess when a disclosure is missing. We evaluate five leading open-weight LLMs (Qwen3-4B, DeepSeek-R1-7B, GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3.5-27B, and Gemma-4-31B) across 518 corporate sustainability reports published between 2010 and 2026 (279,862 text passages). Using a stratified 120-question audit benchmark tested under five controlled evidence conditions (3,000 total responses), we grade every output using an independent referee model (Phi-4-14B) so that no model grades its own family’s work. Three findings stand out for sustainability practi- tioners: (1) models summarize narrative policies reliably (F1 accuracy ≈ 0.729) but struggle to extract exact numerical indicators such as Scope 1 emissions or water withdrawal (F1 ≈ 0.335); (2) even when handed the exact gold-standard page from a report, the strongest model (GPT- OSS-20B) reaches an accuracy ceiling of 0.731, showing that table-reading errors matter more than search errors; and (3) when given a “near-miss” passage from the wrong year or company, standard prompts cause models to invent or substitute numbers in up to 46.7% of cases. By contrast, step-by-step reasoning in DeepSeek-R1-7B catches the mismatch and abstains 77.5% of the time unprompted, while strict audit instructions raise abstention across dense models to 74.2%–80.0%.

candidates.title: Pushing the Limit of Multisite Cooperation via Long-Distance Synergy Over Atomically Dispersed Catalysts.
candidates.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have revolutionized heterogeneous catalysis through near-unity metal utilization and precisely defined active sites. However, their intrinsic limitation-linear scaling relations governing intermediate binding energies on isolated metal centers-fundamentally impedes multifunctional performance in complex multi-step reactions, including the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), CO2 reduction (CO2RR), and nitrate reduction (NO3RR). This review systematically organizes and critically synthesizes an emerging research direction of long-distance synergistic catalysis, wherein nanoscale spatial separation between functional metal species is reframed as a critical, independently tunable design dimension rather than a synthetic deficiency. We deconstruct this frontier mechanistically into two complementary pillars: static electronic synergy-encompassing support-mediated orbital modulation, remote charge shuttling, and neighbor-assisted stabilization without mass transport-and dynamic spillover synergy-involving kinetically facilitated intermediate migration (H*, OH*, NO2-) that mimics enzymatic channeling across segregated sites. Critically underpinned by operando spectroscopy, atomic-resolution microscopy, and first-principles simulations, this framework establishes quantitative distance-performance relationships spanning renewable energy conversion, environmental remediation, and sustainable chemical synthesis. This work provides a mechanistically guided design framework, rather than a universal theory, for next-generation cooperative catalytic architectures transcending single-site constraints.

candidates.title: Application of Social Learning Theory in Teaching Strategies for Students with Special Educational Needs: A Review
candidates.venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Progressive Education and Development
candidates.abstract: Social Learning Theory, developed by Albert Bandura (1977), is one of the most influential theories in understanding how individuals acquire knowledge, skills, and behaviours through social interaction and observation. This review article aims to examine the principles of Social Learning Theory and its application in teaching strategies for students with special educational needs. The review synthesizes findings from previous studies focusing on five core concepts of the theory: observational learning, modelling, imitation, reinforcement, and self-efficacy. The analysis explores how these principles contribute to inclusive education, social competence, behavioural development, academic participation, family involvement, and teacher effectiveness among students with special educational needs. Findings from previous studies indicate that Social Learning Theory provides a valuable framework for supporting inclusive education and promoting positive social, behavioural, and academic outcomes among students with disabilities. Various instructional approaches, including parent-mediated learning, peer modelling, video modelling, positive behaviour support, and self-efficacy enhancement, have been shown to improve communication skills, adaptive behaviours, social interaction, and learning outcomes. The review also highlights the important roles of family involvement and teacher effectiveness in facilitating successful educational experiences for students with special educational needs. Despite its strengths, several limitations were identified, including implementation challenges, resource constraints, and the need to consider cognitive and neurological factors influencing learning. Overall, the findings suggest that Social Learning Theory remains highly relevant in special education and provides a strong foundation for developing effective, inclusive, and evidence-based teaching practices.

candidates.title: Verifiable summarization of electronic health records using large language models to support chart review
candidates.abstract: ObjectivesInformation overload in electronic health records hampers clinicians' ability to efficiently extract and synthesize critical information from a patient's longitudinal health record, leading to increased cognitive burden and delays in care. This study explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) to address this challenge by generating problem-based admission summaries for patients admitted with heart failure, a leading cause of hospitalization worldwide.Materials and methodsWe developed an extract-then-abstract approach guided by disease-specific "summary bundles" to generate summaries of longitudinal clinical notes that prioritize clinically relevant information. Through a mixed-methods evaluation using real-world clinical notes, we compared physicians' ability to answer patient-specific clinical questions with the LLM-generated summaries vs standard chart review.ResultsWhile summary access did not significantly reduce overall questionnaire completion time, frequent summary use significantly contributed to faster questionnaire completion (P = .002). Individual physicians varied in how effectively they leveraged the summaries. Importantly, summary use maintained accuracy in answering clinical questions (88.0% with summaries vs 86.4% without). All physicians indicated they were "likely" or "very likely" to use the summaries in clinical practice, and 87.5% reported that the summaries would save them time. Preferences for summary format varied, highlighting the need for customizable summaries aligned with individual clinician workflows.DiscussionThis exploratory, mixed-methods pilot study provides one of the first extrinsic evaluations of LLMs for longitudinal summarization, demonstrating their potential to enhance clinician efficiency, alleviate workload, and support informed decision-making in time-sensitive care environments.ConclusionOur findings suggest that problem-based longitudinal summarization could improve chart review efficiency and standardize the presentation of clinical information, Variability in summary preferences and use underscores the need for user-centered evaluations to guide the development of LLM-generated summaries that align with clinician workflows.

candidates.title: Human Journey behind Food Is Medicine: A Participatory Study With a Lived Experience Advisory Group
candidates.abstract: BackgroundPoor diet is substantially associated with cardiometabolic diseases in the United States, yet systemic efforts to improve dietary behaviors remain limited. The American Heart Association's Health Care by FoodTM initiative seeks to advance Food Is Medicine interventions by integrating patient-centered insights into program design. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of individuals managing diet-related chronic conditions to better understand the emotional, cultural, and systemic factors influencing dietary behavior change.MethodsUsing a participatory action research approach, a diverse Lived Experience Patient Advisory Group was convened. Fourteen participants engaged in a multiphase process including surveys, daily food diaries, individual interviews, and a 2-day in-person workshop. These activities were designed to elicit personal narratives, identify barriers and motivators to dietary change, and co-develop potential solutions. Thematic analysis was used to synthesize insights across all engagement activities.ResultsFifteen subthemes emerged, grouped into 3 broader themes: facing change, understanding barriers, and acting. These themes highlighted the complex interplay between identity, social norms, access, and self-efficacy in shaping food choices. Participants also proposed a framework of opportunities for intervention, emphasizing the importance of support systems, culturally relevant education, and systemic alignment across health care, community, and policy sectors.ConclusionsBehavior change in food consumption is a deeply personal and socially embedded process. Centering lived experience in Food Is Medicine program design offers critical insights for creating more inclusive, effective, and sustainable interventions. This work underscores the need for coordinated, multilevel strategies to support dietary behavior change at scale.

candidates.title: Teaching the Harness: Student-Aware Skill Transfer for LLM Agents
candidates.abstract: Effective teaching requires reasoning about the learner as well as the task, a capacity that Theory of Mind describes as inferring another agent's latent state from its behavior. We ask whether a stronger LLM teaches a fixed student better when it applies this principle. The student is an LLM agent acting through a harness that fixes its tools, context, and action budget, so a procedure that helps one model can exhaust the budget of another. We introduce Student-Aware Teaching (SAT). The teacher builds a learner model that pairs an empirical profile with hypotheses about the student's limitations, tests these hypotheses with diagnostic probes, and writes reusable skills for the diagnosed failures. A skill enters the library only after it raises success on matched development tasks. With Claude-Sonnet-5 teaching DeepSeek-V4-Flash, SAT reaches 86.46% task success across four primary runs, leading both a profile-free teacher with the same framework (81.04%) and the untaught student (75.00%) in each run. Removing the analytical learner model lowers both prediction and success, and under misleading learner profiles none of the 48 candidate skills passes admission. When DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Gemini-3.8-Flash exchange libraries, each performs better with its own. Saved libraries keep average gains of up to 11.1 points after the teacher leaves. The benefit depends on a student that can follow instructions and a deployment route that delivers them.

candidates.title: ShopMind: A Mental World Model for Personalized and Realistic E-commerce User Simulation
candidates.abstract: Large language models are widely used in e-commerce user simulation, providing a foundation for understanding users and predicting human decisions. However, existing simulators still struggle to achieve both personalization and behavioral realism. Most methods predict the next action directly from interaction histories and the current context, without accounting for the evolving mental world that underlies user behavior. Theory of Mind suggests that behavior is driven by mental states, including beliefs, uncertainties, and intentions. Users may interpret the same information in distinct ways, leading to divergent behaviors, while an individual's mental state evolves through interaction and shapes subsequent actions. Ignoring this process prevents simulators from faithfully capturing individual differences and realistic behavior patterns, and undermines its effectiveness in downstream applications. To address this, we propose ShopMind, a Mental World Model for e-commerce user simulation that captures how consumers interpret shopping information and how their mental states evolve, better reflecting individual users and real-world behavior patterns. We further use behavior-mental state pairs synthesized by ShopMind to train a Mental State Reconstruction (MSR) model, which infers consumers' latent mental states from observable behavior. Experiments show that ShopMind improves personalization by 18.0% and behavioral realism by 19.6% over the strongest alternatives. Moreover, MSR improves performance on consumption value measurement and CTR prediction, showing the utility of ShopMind for understanding and predicting real user behavior.

candidates.title: Deterministic Narrative Gravity: Bridging Theory of Mind and Historical Simulation through ABM-LLM Architectures
candidates.abstract: Historical social simulation faces a fundamental reproducibility challenge: the stochastic nature of large language models (LLMs) introduces a digital butterfly effect that prevents exact replication across multi-turn runs. Furthermore, the inability to control low-level server parameters in commercial LLM hosting environments severely limits reproducibility. To overcome this opacity, we present a deterministic multi-agent framework coupling LLMs to an Agent-Based Modelling (ABM) pipeline grounded in Theory of Mind (ToM) and Cognitive Archaeology, and validate exact artifact identity within local, pinned execution environments using SHA-256 hashing. Run locally at temperature zero with clean per-call model reloads, the system injects differentiated cognitive states per turn through dissonance-driven behavioural modes and gated internal voices. Evaluating seven model configurations spanning 4B to 31B parameters against an ablated baseline reveals clear operational boundaries. Small models ($\leq$8B) suffer from context capacity overload, producing repetitive, specular dialogue loops. However, at $\geq$12B parameters, the ABM scaffolding breaks the monotonous response patterns seen in ablation. Crucially, these scaffolded models exhibit spontaneous diegetic expansion: they coherently expand scenario lore through tactically motivated, anachronism-free details rather than escalating into aggression. By resisting the structural pull toward premature scene closure, scaffolded sessions sustain an open terminal Narrative Vector ($V_N = \mathrm{Open}$ in 12/21 overall; 9/9 in official $\geq$12B configurations) whereas unscaffolded ablation never does (0/21). This framework provides a transparent, auditable benchmark architecture for virtual archaeology, with the full pipeline released as open-source software to enable independent replication.

candidates.title: A Computational Map of the Disaster Mental Health Research Landscape
candidates.abstract: When disasters strike, they not only damage infrastructure, buildings, and the economy, but also affect the mental health of affected populations. Research on the mental health effects of disasters has expanded rapidly and has become an important, well-funded area of psychology, public health, and related social sciences. However, the overall structure of this research landscape has not been systematically characterized. Using large language models, we conducted a review of all articles related to terms 'disaster' and 'mental health' indexed in PubMed. 7,859 articles' metadata were retrieved using the NCBI API, and then Claude Sonnet was used to extract structured variables from the abstracts. The results indicated that earthquakes and epidemics were the most commonly studied disasters while many other disasters such as heat and cold waves have received less attention. PTSD, depression, and anxiety were well investigated but many other mental health issues (e.g., aggression, suicide) are relatively ignored. Despite enjoying relatively large sample sizes (median = 452, IQR = 142 - 1,568), the field rarely utilizes machine learning algorithms. Hypothesis significance testing, reviews, qualitative methods, and structural equation modeling are respectively most common methods while agent-based modeling, machine learning, casual inference, and NLP each appear in less than 1% of articles. Studies are limited to a small number of countries, particularly the United States, Japan, and China, while many disaster-prone regions remain substantially underrepresented. This LLM-assisted computational map provides a broad overview of the disaster mental health literature while highlighting important methodological gaps, with particular emphasis on the underutilization of computational methods that could help advance the field.

candidates.title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
candidates.abstract: Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.

candidates.title: WorldMind: Test-Time Scaling for Visual Spatial Reasoning through Latent World Simulation
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.
